title: Do world models learn global understanding?

paper.title: Do world models learn global understanding?
paper.abstract: Abstract AI systems often feel frustratingly brittle and fragmented. A large language model (LLM) may correctly explain a concept but fail to apply it, or follow safety instructions in one context but not another. This behavior suggests a general failure to lift local information to a global understanding. To gain fundamental insight, we frame “understanding” as learning constraints and propagating their consequences. We construct learning tasks on monoid worlds, sets of states connected by action transitions ( state , action , next state ) (\text{state},\text{action},\text{next state}) , where observed training transitions and an underlying unseen constraint jointly determine held-out transitions. Measuring generalization tests whether models can learn global constraints from local transitions and propagate their consequences. We consider inverse, commutativity, composition, and periodicity constraints relevant to spatial and semantic structure. Across attention, recurrent, and state-space architectures, next-state training on paths of observed transitions fits the data but fails to propagate non-trivial constraints. Compositional training, which uses identical paths but hides intermediate states from the input, achieves 96 % 96\% accuracy on inverse, commutativity, and composition constraints across architectures, yields corresponding improvements in geometric generalization of world models trained on embodied environments ( + 42 % +42\% on propagating commutative constraints) and relational generalization in Wikidata-finetuned LLMs ( + 73 % +73\% on composition propagation). How far do models propagate constraints when inferring an unseen fact may depend on first inferring others? We define proof depth d d of a held-out transition, measuring the minimum number of inference rounds to infer the transition, and find that model generalization decreases sharply with increasing proof depth. A compositionally trained transformer on length T = 2 T=2 paths generalizes at 95 % 95\% for transitions derivable directly from observations ( d = 1 d=1 ) but only at 49 % 49\% for those requiring an additional inference round ( d = 2 d=2 ). Increasing compositional path length T T improves generalization, and T = 4 T=4 compositional models achieve 95 % 95\% accuracy on d = 2 d=2 transitions. These results provide a formal way to investigate global understanding in language and world models and demonstrate that compositional training promotes information propagation and integration.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: What does it mean for a system to understand? Do language models understand semantics when training on “Tom’s parent is Mary” fails to teach “Mary’s child is Tom” ( Berglund et al., 2024 ) ? Do world models understand space if a left rotation followed by a right rotation produces a new scene ( Kwon et al., 2026 ) ? In both cases, a constraint (parent and child are converses; left and right rotations are inverses) lets a few seen facts determine many unseen ones. This suggests framing “understanding” as learning constraints and propagating their consequences globally. To study constraint learning and propagation systematically, we construct monoid worlds where constraints are controllable and propagation consequences can be mathematically determined. A monoid world is a set of states with actions defining transitions between states. In the context of space, the set could be points on a line, and the actions, left / right \text{left}/\text{right} , could correspond to opposite translations. These spatial actions satisfy an inverse constraint: moving left and then right returns you to the original state. Analogously, semantic relations obey constraints like composition: the parent of a parent is a grandparent. We capture these constraints as equalities over action sequences, enabling us to determine from data, manipulate, and directly specify a large class of constraints governing each world. Since our world is precisely defined, we can directly evaluate whether models propagate constraints by constructing held-out sets of transitions which are uniquely determined (semantically entailed) by joint knowledge of the constraint and observed transitions. For example, observing ( 1 , left , 2 ) (1,\text{left},2) entails the unseen transition ( 2 , right , 1 ) (2,\text{right},1) when the constraint left = right − 1 \text{left}=\text{right}^{-1} is learned. Generalization determines whether models learn constraints from data and propagate their consequences. Not all consequences of constraints are created equal, and some require multiple inference steps. Consider learning a new fact which sets in motion a chain of factual updates. We frame this formally by defining a miniature proof system and measure the inference complexity of an unseen transition by its proof depth d d : the minimum number of rounds in our system to derive the transition. We construct worlds with unseen transitions with varied proof depths and explore how generalization and training dynamics change with the required inference depth. Next-state training on paths of monoid transitions fails to propagate non-trivial constraints across transformer, recurrent, and state-space models. Compositional training, learning action compositions by hiding intermediate state inputs, improves generalization across worlds at an average accuracy of 96 % 96\% on inverse, commutative, and composition constraints. We apply our monoid framing to study constraint propagation in learning visual environments with world models and relational structure with pretrained large language models (LLMs). We find traditional next-state-style objectives poorly propagate geometric and semantic constraints, while compositional training improves generalization by + 42 % +42\% on commutative constraints and + 73 % +73\% on composition constraints. Finally, we find that generalization decreases sharply with proof depth d d , implying that models struggle to iteratively apply constraints. Increasing compositional path length T T , however, improves deeper propagation.

sections.heading: 2 A monoid framework for global constraints
sections.text: We construct worlds governed by specified constraints and hold out transitions which are jointly implied by observed transitions and associated constraints. We train models on paths of observed transitions and evaluate them on held-out transitions, measuring a model’s ability to learn global constraints from local data and propagate their consequences.

sections.heading: 2.1 Monoid world and global constraints
sections.text: A monoid world is a finite set of states 𝒮 := [ N ] := { 0 , … , N − 1 } \mathcal{S}:=[N]:=\{0,\dots,N-1\} with actions 𝒜 := { a 0 , … , a n − 1 } \mathcal{A}:=\{a_{0},\dots,a_{n-1}\} , each a function a : 𝒮 → 𝒮 a:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S} on the state space. Consider the world shown in Figure 1 a, which has a discrete 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} rotation interpretation with states 𝒮 := [ 4 ] \mathcal{S}:=[4] and actions L : x ↦ x − 1 mod 4 L:x\mapsto x-1\mod 4 and R : x ↦ x + 1 mod 4 R:x\mapsto x+1\mod 4 . Actions can be composed to form action sequences, and with the identity action 1 1 , form a monoid. Local observations are transitions ( s , a , a ⁡ ( s ) ) (s,a,a(s)) , which correspond to the change of state s ∈ 𝒮 s\in\mathcal{S} under the action a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} . In our rotation world, ( 0 , R , 1 ) (0,R,1) is a transition. The global constraints of our monoid world are equality relations between action sequences: two distinct sequences of actions induce the same map on the entire state space. In other words, at every initial state, the paths of transitions for the two action sequences converge to the same terminal state. The global nature comes from the requirement that the constraint on transitions applies uniformly over the entire state space. In our rotation world, we have two essential constraints: inverse L ​ R = R ​ L = 1 LR=RL=1 and periodicity L 4 = 1 L^{4}=1 , from which all other constraints are derived. When building a monoid world with a specified constraint, we choose a state-space size N N and randomly sample action transitions a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} such that the constraint is satisfied. For example, when constructing inverse worlds L ​ R = R ​ L = 1 LR=RL=1 as in Figure 1 a, we choose L : 𝒮 → 𝒮 L:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S} as a random bijection and derive R R as its inverse. Monoid theory warns us that finite worlds may inadvertently introduce unwanted constraints, so we audit all our worlds by enumerating u = v u=v global constraints for | u | + | v | ≤ 8 |u|+|v|\leq 8 and reject impure worlds. We explore inverse, commutativity, composition, periodicity, and copy constraints shown as a presentation, ⟨ Actions ∣ Constraints ⟩ \langle\text{Actions}\mid\text{Constraints}\rangle , in Figure 2 . sections.heading: 2.2 Evaluation of constraint propagation by entailed hold-outs
sections.text: We hold out transitions which are jointly inferable from observed training transitions and the world’s global constraint. Formally, inferability is captured by semantic entailment. A transition t = ( s , a , s ′ ) t=(s,a,s^{\prime}) is semantically entailed by constraint 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and seen transitions 𝒯 \mathcal{T} if and only if all possible assignments of transitions that satisfy 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and agree on 𝒯 \mathcal{T} also agree on t t . Consider the cyclic inverse world in Figure 1 a. The unseen transition t = ( 1 , R , 2 ) t=(1,R,2) is semantically entailed since any world that contains the seen transition ( 2 , L , 1 ) ∈ 𝒯 (2,L,1)\in\mathcal{T} and the inverse constraint must agree on t t . In practice, we perform greedy sampling with semantic entailment checks until we reach a specified hold-out size.

sections.heading: 2.3 Next-state and compositional training
sections.text: We train models on paths of (T) transitions, ( s 0 , a 0 , s 1 , … , a T − 1 , s T ) (s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},\ldots,a_{T-1},s_{T}) , where s t + 1 = a t ​ ( s t ) s_{t+1}=a_{t}(s_{t}) . At each step we sample uniformly from training transitions originating from the current state. Every transition in the training path belongs to the training set of transitions (no held-out transition is ever shown). Models receive only paths of observed local transitions, never the global constraint directly. Under next-state training, we show intermediate states as inputs and for steps 1 ≤ t ≤ T 1\leq t\leq T train to predict s t s_{t} given ( s 0 , a 0 , s 1 , … , s t − 1 , a t − 1 ) (s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},\dots,s_{t-1},a_{t-1}) as input (Figure 1 c). Under compositional training, we hide intermediate states from the inputs and for 1 ≤ t ≤ T 1\leq t\leq T train to predict s t s_{t} given ( s 0 , a 0 , a 1 , … , a t − 1 ) (s_{0},a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{t-1}) as input, forcing the model to compose actions internally with T T controlling the composition length. At T = 1 T=1 , next-state and compositional training coincide.

sections.heading: 2.4 Measuring inference complexity of a transition with proof depth
sections.text: Certain held-out transitions are intuitively harder to infer than others. In the commutative world of Figure 4 , both held-out transitions are semantically entailed, but only one can be immediately derived from observed transitions; the other requires first inferring an intermediate transition. We quantify this dependency by proof depth, defined relative to a fixed set of inference rules based on the world’s algebraic constraints. Consider the rules of the commutative world depicted in Figure 4 b. Knowing transitions ( 1 , F , 0 ) , ( 0 , R , 2 ) (1,F,0),(0,R,2) , and ( 1 , R , 3 ) (1,R,3) derives ( 3 , F , 2 ) (3,F,2) since actions F F and R R commute, so the paths 1 → 𝐹 0 → 𝑅 2 1\xrightarrow{F}0\xrightarrow{R}2 and 1 → 𝑅 3 → 𝐹 2 1\xrightarrow{R}3\xrightarrow{F}2 must end at the same state. Constraint cascading then happens in rounds, each round using the derived transitions of previous rounds, then inference rules infer transitions (Figure 4 b). The minimal number of rounds to infer a transition is its proof depth.

sections.heading: 3 Constraint propagation in controlled monoid worlds
sections.text: We construct monoid worlds with N = 1024 N=1024 states satisfying specified constraints and train models on 95 % 95\% of state-action transitions ( s , a , a ⁡ ( s ) ) (s,a,a(s)) such that the remaining 5 % 5\% of held-out transitions, which we evaluate model generalization on, are entailed by seen transitions and the world’s constraint. Unless stated otherwise, models have four layers of width 64 and train for 150 150 k steps at T = 2 T=2 with reported results averaged over five seeds.

sections.heading: 3.1 Next-state training fails to propagate constraints
sections.text: Under a next-state objective, where intermediate states are shown, transformers on inverse worlds fail to generalize with accuracy at chance (Figure 1 d.1). Scaling model, world, and compute does not save next-state training, and models continue to fail at propagating inverse constraints (Appendix A ). Across attention, recurrent, and state-space architectures, next-state training T = 2 T=2 fails, indistinguishable from chance, at propagating inverse, commutative, composition, and periodicity constraints in their associated worlds (Figure 2 ). Only in the trivial copy world where actions are identical ( A = B A=B ) does next-state training generalize. We find a systematic “copy” failure mode of general constraint propagation by next-state trained models, where models behave as if every world were the copy world. Averaged across architectures and worlds, 64 % 64\% of incorrectly inferred unseen transitions are explained by copy propagation, assuming the unseen ( s , A , A ⁡ ( s ) ) (s,A,A(s)) transition matches seen ( s , B , B ⁡ ( s ) ) (s,B,B(s)) , although seen transitions contradict the A = B A=B constraint at almost every state (Appendix B ). These results suggest the next-state objective poorly propagates constraints from data.

sections.heading: 3.2 Compositional training improves constraint propagation
sections.text: Figure 2: Across monoid worlds and architectures, compositional training generalizes better than next-state training with equal optimizer steps. Compositional objective propagates inverse, commutative, and composition constraints with average accuracy of 96 % 96\% , and copy at 100 % 100\% . Next-state training only succeeds on copy and fails on other tested families. Neither propagates periodicity. Points averaged over 5 seeds and bars show standard deviations. Under a compositional objective, where intermediate states are hidden, transformers successfully propagate inverse constraints, generalizing unseen transitions with ≥ 93 % \geq 93\% accuracy (Figure 1 d.1). We find a sharp jump in generalization of 98 % 98\% when varying the composition length from T = 1 T=1 , a reduction to next-state training, to T = 2 T=2 , when training first includes two-action compositions. Across architectures, compositional training at T = 2 T=2 enables models to propagate inverse, commutativity, and composition constraints with an average accuracy of 96 % 96\% and copy at 100 % 100\% (Figure 2 ). Extending composition length to T = 4 T=4 yields nearly identical generalization results of 96 % 96\% averaged over the same worlds (Appendix D ). Periodicity constraints, however, are not propagated by next-state or compositional training at T = 2 ​ or ​ 4 T=2\text{ or }4 . Across periodicity worlds A k = 1 A^{k}=1 for k = 3 , 4 , 5 k=3,4,5 , compositionally trained transformers at 1 ≤ T ≤ 8 1\leq T\leq 8 all fail to generalize, suggesting that the failure is not due to training paths too short to contain the constraint. Compositionally trained models also have reduced “copy” failure modes, hallucinating a copy constraint for 36 % 36\% of failures (Appendix B ). Compositional training fits observed transitions an order of magnitude earlier than it recovers held-out ones. On the inverse world, transformers learn 100 % 100\% of seen transitions at 1.2 1.2 k steps but achieve 50 % 50\% generalization at 16 16 k, approximately 13 13 times as many training steps, evidence of a grokking-like delay ( Power et al., 2022 ) . Finally, generalization accuracy, fixing world size, increases monotonically with “constraint evidence”, the number of seen transitions satisfying the constraint (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 4 Constraint propagation in vision and language
sections.text: Figure 3: Compositional objectives improve constraint propagation over next-state-style training in vision and language a) 1) AI2-THOR virtual 3D environment, where an embodied agent translates between observed states. Inverse L ​ R = R ​ L = 1 LR=RL=1 and commutative F ​ R = R ​ F FR=RF constraints hold approximately due to collisions. 2) Training and evaluation follow Figure 1 c with image observations replacing abstract states. 3) Next-observation training marginally outperforms pixel-shifting baseline ( + 8 % +8\% ) while compositional training improves by ( + 46 % +46\% ) (observation). Training to predict state, minimizing visual cues, collapses next-state generalization to chance, while compositional training generalizes with 96 % 96\% (state). Results averaged over three seeds. b) 1) Wikidata knowledge graph world, where entities are states and relations are multi-valued actions. 2) LLMs are finetuned with next-token prediction, the objective changing the sentence phrasing. 3) Compositional, not next-state, phrasing propagates inverse constraint at average accuracy of 45 % 45\% and composition at 73 % 73\% . We explore learning and propagating constraints towards geometric generalization in world models trained on visual environments and relational generalization in LLMs trained on knowledge-based tasks. We identify domain-relevant constraints, which often hold only approximately, and build entailed hold-outs which test whether models propagate the constraints.

sections.heading: 4.1 Geometric constraints in visual world models
sections.text: An agent moves (L)eft/(R)ight/(F)orward/(B)ackward through an AI2-THOR virtual environment, generating a dataset of observation-action paths of length T = 2 T=2 (Figure 3 a.1) ( Kolve et al., 2022 ) . Euclidean geometry imposes constraints on motion requiring that the final destination be independent of the order of translations: stepping forward and then right or right and then forward takes you to the same endpoint. Actions are also invertible since you can undo a previous action by stepping in the opposite direction. In environments with object collisions, these constraints do not hold for all states. We can compute these approximate constraints by identifying paths which start from the same initial observation and recording whether certain action sequences converge to the same endpoint observation. If two action sequences frequently ( ≥ 50 % \geq 50\% ) map between the same initial and terminal observations, we declare them an approximate constraint. We find the Euclidean constraints: inverse L ​ R = 1 LR=1 and commutativity F ​ R = R ​ F FR=RF , which hold roughly 80 % 80\% of the time. We hold out transitions ( obs , action , next obs ) (\text{obs},\text{action},\text{next obs}) that test propagation of inverse and commutative constraints. These hold-outs are taken at states away from object collisions where constraints are valid. Transformer world models are trained to predict the next observation given previous observations and actions. Accuracy is measured by choosing the observation in the dataset with the highest predicted likelihood. Since visual similarity may enable held-out recovery without learning geometric constraints, we compare to a baseline of shifting observation pixels. Under next-observation training, where intermediate observations are shown, world models poorly generalize inverse and commutative constraints, with an accuracy of only 50 % 50\% and 51 % 51\% , respectively, compared to the pixel-shift baseline of 41 % 41\% and 44 % 44\% (Figure 3 a.2, 3 a.3). Trained compositionally, hiding intermediate observations, world models achieve 83 % 83\% accuracy on inverse and 93 % 93\% on commutative constraints, averaging a + 38 % +38\% improvement over next-observation trained models. To examine recovery without visual shortcuts, we train transformers to predict the next state directly, instead of its observation. Generalization for next-state trained models on inverse and commutative constraints collapses to random guessing, while compositionally trained models achieve 94 % 94\% and 98 % 98\% , respectively (Figure 3 a.3). These results suggest next-observation/state training poorly propagates inverse and commutative constraints in visual domains while compositional training successfully propagates geometric constraints even without visual cues.

sections.heading: 4.2 Relational constraints in large language models
sections.text: We examine when LLMs, trained on facts, propagate relational constraints without premises supplied in context. We study inverse constraints between successor and predecessor, the converse relation between parent and child, and the composition of parent and grandparent. Unlike inverse relations, converse relations branch, and the child of a parent may be a sibling, not necessarily a strict identity. For each constraint, we extract a Wikidata knowledge graph of 512 512 renamed individuals and associated relations (Figure 3 b.1). We hold out transitions ( person A , relation , person B ) (\text{person A},\text{relation},\text{person B}) jointly entailed by training transitions and constraint. For example, the observed relationship ( Dana , parent , Ines ) (\text{Dana},\text{parent},\text{Ines}) entails the held-out relationship ( Ines , child , Dana ) (\text{Ines},\text{child},\text{Dana}) under the converse constraint. We finetune pretrained base LLMs (270M to 4B parameters) with next-token prediction on natural-language sentences generated from (T=2) training paths. We compare two phrasings the same underlying path. Next-state phrasing allows models to condition on intermediate entities, e.g., “Dana’s parent is Ines, whose parent is Vera”, while compositional phrasing omits intermediate entities, “Dana’s parent’s parent is Vera” (Figure 3 b.2). Unlike previous compositional objectives, next-token prediction over compositional phrasing never uses intermediate entities as targets, so we include (T=1) paths in both conditions. We evaluate on a held-out relation such as ( Ines , child , Dana ) (\text{Ines},\text{child},\text{Dana}) by prompting “Ines’s child is” and choosing the highest-likelihood name from the graph. For relations with multiple correct answers (converse and grandparent), we report filtered accuracy where all other correct answers (e.g., Dana’s siblings) are excluded from the likelihood comparison. Training with next-state phrasing fails to propagate inverse and composition constraints with an average generalization of 1 % 1\% , marginally better than random guessing (Figure 3 b.3). Compositional phrasing improves inverse propagation with an average accuracy of 45 % 45\% and composition generalization at 73 % 73\% . Converse is not propagated by next-state or compositional methods. Composition learning over paths presents a shortcut: while “Dana’s grandparent is Vera” is never shown during training, models see the T = 2 T=2 path “Dana’s parent is Ines, whose parent is Vera” under next-state phrasing and “Dana’s parent’s parent is Vera” under compositional phrasing. Can propagation still occur when such shortcut paths are removed? We train a transformer on T = 2 T=2 paths in the monoid composition world N = 1024 N=1024 with and without shortcuts (Appendix F ). Next-state trained models fail in both settings, while compositionally trained models still recover without shortcuts ( 50 % 50\% versus 92 % 92\% with shortcuts). These results suggest that while shortcuts help compositionally trained models recover, they are not required for composition propagation. To understand the effect of branching on converse constraint propagation, we construct an N = 1024 N=1024 branching world that interpolates between line β = 0 \beta=0 , where parent and child are true inverses, and binary tree β = 1 \beta=1 , where each parent has two children and only a converse relationship remains (Appendix E ). For comparison, parents in our Wikidata world have an average of 2.5 2.5 children. A transformer trained compositionally with T = 2 T=2 achieves 99 % 99\% on β = 0 \beta=0 , but adding only a 10 % 10\% chance a parent might have another child ( β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 ) drops accuracy to 63 % 63\% and ≤ 3 % \leq 3\% for β ≥ 0.75 \beta\geq 0.75 . Compositional phrasing improves inverse and composition constraint propagation but is limited in converse generalization on branching worlds.

Previous results concerned only d = 1 d=1 generalization. We now explore the effect of proof depth on constraint propagation by compositionally trained transformers. sections.heading: 5.1 Constraint propagation decreases sharply with proof depth
sections.text: We find generalization of compositionally trained models decreases sharply with proof depth, while next-state trained models do not generalize at any proof depth. A transformer trained with composition length T = 2 T=2 recovers d = 1 d=1 transitions, whose derivation depends directly on seen transitions, at 95 % 95\% , while d = 2 d=2 recovery, transitions whose derivation also depends on unseen d = 1 d=1 transitions, is only at 49 % 49\% . The steep decreasing trend in generalization continues to deeper transitions with d = 3 d=3 at 15 % 15\% , d = 4 d=4 at 5 % 5\% , and d = 5 d=5 onward indistinguishable from random chance. Similar step-to-step accuracy ratios over depths 1 ≤ d ≤ 4 1\leq d\leq 4 suggest approximate geometric decay with rate 0.4 ± 0.1 0.4\pm 0.1 . Even with compositional training, models struggle to propagate constraints deeply.

sections.heading: 5.2 Propagation dynamics suggest internal constraint cascades
sections.text: Models trained compositionally propagate constraints to infer transitions iteratively by proof depth: first d = 1 d=1 transitions are learned, then d = 2 d=2 , d = 3 d=3 , and so on (Figure 4 d). Transformers trained with composition length T = 4 T=4 reach half their final accuracy for d = 1 d=1 at 26 26 k training steps, d = 2 d=2 at 50 50 k steps, d = 3 d=3 at 102 102 k, and d = 4 d=4 at 236 236 k, so each depth takes about twice as many steps as the one before ( 2.1 × 2.1\times , geometric mean). Monotonic ordering holds for all 1 ≤ d ≤ 8 1\leq d\leq 8 , but spacing beyond d = 4 d=4 shrinks, and d = 5 d=5 to d = 8 d=8 all reach half their final accuracy between 364 364 k and 376 376 k steps. Timing suggests that models may be propagating constraints in a qualitatively similar way to constraint cascades, where local rules are applied repeatedly to derive held-out transitions in order of proof depth d d . Unlike general constraint propagation, a cascade predicts that transitions are inferred only after all their derivation premises, the other unseen transitions required for the derivation, are inferred (Figure 4 b). We examine 150 150 checkpoints for each of 5 5 seeds trained over composition lengths T = 2 , 3 , 4 T=2,3,4 on the commutative world to find the percentage of inferred transitions missing their derivation premises. To remove timing confounds (on average d = n + 1 d=n+1 is learned after d = n d=n ), we compare to a null which shuffles the identity of d = n d=n transitions, preserving the timing but removing any dependency structure. We find that only 3 % 3\% of correct inferences made by the transformer were made without having correctly inferred their derivation premises, compared to 11 % 11\% for the null model, a difference of 3.7 × 3.7\times . Throughout training, the model’s correct held-out predictions are almost always derivable from seen transitions and other predictions, satisfying the constraint cascade condition.

sections.heading: 5.3 Longer composition length enables deeper propagation
sections.text: Training on longer composition lengths T T with the same number of training steps improves generalization at higher proof depths (Figure 4 c). Increasing T T from 2 2 to 3 3 maintains d = 1 d=1 recovery at ≥ 95 % \geq 95\% but significantly improves d = 2 d=2 by + 43 % +43\% and similarly improves recovery of 3 ≤ d ≤ 8 3\leq d\leq 8 with an average increase of + 19 % +19\% . Raising composition length T T from 3 3 to 4 4 maintains d = 1 d=1 and d = 2 d=2 recovery while again accumulating improvement for 3 ≤ d ≤ 8 3\leq d\leq 8 over T = 3 T=3 by + 14 % +14\% . Decay curves also change qualitatively, from the geometric-like decay of T = 2 T=2 , which is indistinguishable from random guessing by d = 5 d=5 , to plateau-like behavior at T = 3 T=3 and T = 4 T=4 , where generalization appears to flatten out at roughly 10 % 10\% and 20 % 20\% , respectively. These results suggest training on longer composition lengths may be key to deep propagation of constraints.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Identical data, learned under a different objective, can turn a model that fails to generalize into one that learns and propagates global constraints. Across attention, recurrent, and state-space architectures, compositionally trained models propagate non-trivial constraints to recover unseen data while next-state trained models do not. Compositional training also shows superior propagation in vision and language domains. Both objectives use identical path data, the only difference is that compositional training hides intermediate states. Global understanding therefore depends on how training requires local observations to be combined. Providing intermediate states encourages models to solve the task locally, while compositional training encourages integration across actions. Training objective, perhaps more than architecture or task domain, determines whether a model propagates certain constraints. Across monoid worlds, constraints that are (not) propagated are consistently (not) propagated across the disparate architectures tested. Similarly, constraints propagated compositionally in monoid worlds are also propagated by compositional approaches in visual and language domains. This pattern suggests that controlled monoid worlds capture general learning biases that extend to richer tasks and may provide simplified environments for understanding and designing better-propagating algorithms. Even when models propagate constraints, propagation is shallow, with generalization decreasing sharply with proof depth. Higher proof depth transitions are also recovered later and more slowly. Together with training dynamics, this suggests an internal process resembling a slow, inaccurate constraint cascade. Increasing composition length improves generalization to deeper consequences, suggesting that propagation reach depends on the organization of local information it learns from. Propagating constraint consequences deeply is essential for consistent information integration.

sections.heading: 7 Related work
sections.text: LLMs often learn facts without propagating their consequences. The reversal curse shows that training on one direction of a relation can fail to recover its reverse ( Berglund et al., 2024 ) . Similar failures exist in implicit reasoning, where models poorly compose relations ( Balesni et al., 2025 ) . Changes to training can address individual failures such as reversal ( Ma et al., 2026 ) and composition ( Feng et al., 2025 ) have been proposed, but remain specialized. We frame these failures and improvements in the context of learning and propagating constraints. Across controlled monoid worlds, visual environments, and knowledge-based language tasks, we study how objective determines which constraints models propagate. We further measure how far consequences are propagated using proof depth and explore associated training dynamics. Accurate local predictions do not imply coherent global understanding ( Vafa et al., 2024 ) . Previous work improves consistency through reverse-prediction training ( Kwon et al., 2026 ) or architectural modifications that recover group structures in synthetic environments ( Keurti et al., 2023 ) . Our constraint propagation framework extends beyond group structure to include semantic constraints such as the converse relation between parent and child. Training without intermediate states has improved generalization in knowledge-graph embedding models ( Guu et al., 2015 ) and discouraged local prediction shortcuts in planning ( Bachmann and Nagarajan, 2024 ) . We study how training objective affects constraint propagation across architectures, visual environments, and language tasks. Compositional training improves propagation for many geometric and semantic constraints but fails on others. Even when immediate consequences are recovered, generalization decreases sharply with proof depth. Composition length increases propagation reach to higher proof depths, suggesting that how much local information models combine during training shapes how far they propagate what they learn.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We frame global understanding as learning constraints from local observations and propagating their consequences deeply. Our monoid worlds provide controlled environments where generalization is entailed by observed data and unobserved global constraints. Across architectures, next-state training fails to propagate non-trivial constraints, while compositional training substantially improves propagation. We apply our constraint framing to visual and language tasks and find corresponding improvements under compositional-style objectives as well as regularities in which constraints propagate and under what conditions across domains. Deep propagation remains limited, though longer composition lengths help. These results suggest that global understanding requires training methods that encourage models to integrate local observations and deeply propagate their consequences.

Alexander Detkov & Matt Thomson Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Affiliation: Pasadena, CA 91125, USA Email: {adetkov,matt}@caltech.edu Abstract AI systems often feel frustratingly brittle and fragmented. A large language model (LLM) may correctly explain a concept but fail to apply it, or follow safety instructions in one context but not another. This behavior suggests a general failure to lift local information to a global understanding. To gain fundamental insight, we frame “understanding” as learning constraints and propagating their consequences. We construct learning tasks on monoid worlds, sets of states connected by action transitions ( state , action , next state ) (\text{state},\text{action},\text{next state}) , where observed training transitions and an underlying unseen constraint jointly determine held-out transitions. Measuring generalization tests whether models can learn global constraints from local transitions and propagate their consequences. We consider inverse, commutativity, composition, and periodicity constraints relevant to spatial and semantic structure. Across attention, recurrent, and state-space architectures, next-state training on paths of observed transitions fits the data but fails to propagate non-trivial constraints. Compositional training, which uses identical paths but hides intermediate states from the input, achieves 96 % 96\% accuracy on inverse, commutativity, and composition constraints across architectures, yields corresponding improvements in geometric generalization of world models trained on embodied environments ( + 42 % +42\% on propagating commutative constraints) and relational generalization in Wikidata-finetuned LLMs ( + 73 % +73\% on composition propagation). How far do models propagate constraints when inferring an unseen fact may depend on first inferring others? We define proof depth d d of a held-out transition, measuring the minimum number of inference rounds to infer the transition, and find that model generalization decreases sharply with increasing proof depth. A compositionally trained transformer on length T = 2 T=2 paths generalizes at 95 % 95\% for transitions derivable directly from observations ( d = 1 d=1 ) but only at 49 % 49\% for those requiring an additional inference round ( d = 2 d=2 ). Increasing compositional path length T T improves generalization, and T = 4 T=4 compositional models achieve 95 % 95\% accuracy on d = 2 d=2 transitions. These results provide a formal way to investigate global understanding in language and world models and demonstrate that compositional training promotes information propagation and integration. 1 Introduction What does it mean for a system to understand? Do language models understand semantics when training on “Tom’s parent is Mary” fails to teach “Mary’s child is Tom” ( Berglund et al., 2024 ) ? Do world models understand space if a left rotation followed by a right rotation produces a new scene ( Kwon et al., 2026 ) ? In both cases, a constraint (parent and child are converses; left and right rotations are inverses) lets a few seen facts determine many unseen ones. This suggests framing “understanding” as learning constraints and propagating their consequences globally. To study constraint learning and propagation systematically, we construct monoid worlds where constraints are controllable and propagation consequences can be mathematically determined. A monoid world is a set of states with actions defining transitions between states. In the context of space, the set could be points on a line, and the actions, left / right \text{left}/\text{right} , could correspond to opposite translations. These spatial actions satisfy an inverse constraint: moving left and then right returns you to the original state. Analogously, semantic relations obey constraints like composition: the parent of a parent is a grandparent. We capture these constraints as equalities over action sequences, enabling us to determine from data, manipulate, and directly specify a large class of constraints governing each world. Since our world is precisely defined, we can directly evaluate whether models propagate constraints by constructing held-out sets of transitions which are uniquely determined (semantically entailed) by joint knowledge of the constraint and observed transitions. For example, observing ( 1 , left , 2 ) (1,\text{left},2) entails the unseen transition ( 2 , right , 1 ) (2,\text{right},1) when the constraint left = right − 1 \text{left}=\text{right}^{-1} is learned. Generalization determines whether models learn constraints from data and propagate their consequences. Not all consequences of constraints are created equal, and some require multiple inference steps. Consider learning a new fact which sets in motion a chain of factual updates. We frame this formally by defining a miniature proof system and measure the inference complexity of an unseen transition by its proof depth d d : the minimum number of rounds in our system to derive the transition. We construct worlds with unseen transitions with varied proof depths and explore how generalization and training dynamics change with the required inference depth. Next-state training on paths of monoid transitions fails to propagate non-trivial constraints across transformer, recurrent, and state-space models. Compositional training, learning action compositions by hiding intermediate state inputs, improves generalization across worlds at an average accuracy of 96 % 96\% on inverse, commutative, and composition constraints. We apply our monoid framing to study constraint propagation in learning visual environments with world models and relational structure with pretrained large language models (LLMs). We find traditional next-state-style objectives poorly propagate geometric and semantic constraints, while compositional training improves generalization by + 42 % +42\% on commutative constraints and + 73 % +73\% on composition constraints. Finally, we find that generalization decreases sharply with proof depth d d , implying that models struggle to iteratively apply constraints. Increasing compositional path length T T , however, improves deeper propagation. 2 A monoid framework for global constraints We construct worlds governed by specified constraints and hold out transitions which are jointly implied by observed transitions and associated constraints. We train models on paths of observed transitions and evaluate them on held-out transitions, measuring a model’s ability to learn global constraints from local data and propagate their consequences. 2.1 Monoid world and global constraints A monoid world is a finite set of states 𝒮 := [ N ] := { 0 , … , N − 1 } \mathcal{S}:=[N]:=\{0,\dots,N-1\} with actions 𝒜 := { a 0 , … , a n − 1 } \mathcal{A}:=\{a_{0},\dots,a_{n-1}\} , each a function a : 𝒮 → 𝒮 a:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S} on the state space. Consider the world shown in Figure 1 a, which has a discrete 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} rotation interpretation with states 𝒮 := [ 4 ] \mathcal{S}:=[4] and actions L : x ↦ x − 1 mod 4 L:x\mapsto x-1\mod 4 and R : x ↦ x + 1 mod 4 R:x\mapsto x+1\mod 4 . Actions can be composed to form action sequences, and with the identity action 1 1 , form a monoid. Local observations are transitions ( s , a , a ⁡ ( s ) ) (s,a,a(s)) , which correspond to the change of state s ∈ 𝒮 s\in\mathcal{S} under the action a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} . In our rotation world, ( 0 , R , 1 ) (0,R,1) is a transition. The global constraints of our monoid world are equality relations between action sequences: two distinct sequences of actions induce the same map on the entire state space. In other words, at every initial state, the paths of transitions for the two action sequences converge to the same terminal state. The global nature comes from the requirement that the constraint on transitions applies uniformly over the entire state space. In our rotation world, we have two essential constraints: inverse L ​ R = R ​ L = 1 LR=RL=1 and periodicity L 4 = 1 L^{4}=1 , from which all other constraints are derived. When building a monoid world with a specified constraint, we choose a state-space size N N and randomly sample action transitions a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} such that the constraint is satisfied. For example, when constructing inverse worlds L ​ R = R ​ L = 1 LR=RL=1 as in Figure 1 a, we choose L : 𝒮 → 𝒮 L:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S} as a random bijection and derive R R as its inverse. Monoid theory warns us that finite worlds may inadvertently introduce unwanted constraints, so we audit all our worlds by enumerating u = v u=v global constraints for | u | + | v | ≤ 8 |u|+|v|\leq 8 and reject impure worlds. We explore inverse, commutativity, composition, periodicity, and copy constraints shown as a presentation, ⟨ Actions ∣ Constraints ⟩ \langle\text{Actions}\mid\text{Constraints}\rangle , in Figure 2 . Figure 1: Toy instantiation of an inverse monoid world with training and evaluation setup. a) A four-state world with actions L L and R R satisfying inverse constraint L ​ R = R ​ L = 1 LR=RL=1 , seen and unseen transitions, and sample training path. b) Constraint propagation uses seen transitions and the constraint to infer unseen transitions. c) Next-state training shows intermediate states, while compositional training does not. Evaluation is generalization over unseen transitions. d) 1) Next-state training fails to propagate inverse constraint, while compositional training succeeds ( ≥ 93 % \geq 93\% ). 2) Training curves for T = 2 T=2 show sharp grokking-like generalization. Plots averaged over 5 seeds. 2.2 Evaluation of constraint propagation by entailed hold-outs We hold out transitions which are jointly inferable from observed training transitions and the world’s global constraint. Formally, inferability is captured by semantic entailment. A transition t = ( s , a , s ′ ) t=(s,a,s^{\prime}) is semantically entailed by constraint 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and seen transitions 𝒯 \mathcal{T} if and only if all possible assignments of transitions that satisfy 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and agree on 𝒯 \mathcal{T} also agree on t t . Consider the cyclic inverse world in Figure 1 a. The unseen transition t = ( 1 , R , 2 ) t=(1,R,2) is semantically entailed since any world that contains the seen transition ( 2 , L , 1 ) ∈ 𝒯 (2,L,1)\in\mathcal{T} and the inverse constraint must agree on t t . In practice, we perform greedy sampling with semantic entailment checks until we reach a specified hold-out size. 2.3 Next-state and compositional training We train models on paths of (T) transitions, ( s 0 , a 0 , s 1 , … , a T − 1 , s T ) (s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},\ldots,a_{T-1},s_{T}) , where s t + 1 = a t ​ ( s t ) s_{t+1}=a_{t}(s_{t}) . At each step we sample uniformly from training transitions originating from the current state. Every transition in the training path belongs to the training set of transitions (no held-out transition is ever shown). Models receive only paths of observed local transitions, never the global constraint directly. Under next-state training, we show intermediate states as inputs and for steps 1 ≤ t ≤ T 1\leq t\leq T train to predict s t s_{t} given ( s 0 , a 0 , s 1 , … , s t − 1 , a t − 1 ) (s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},\dots,s_{t-1},a_{t-1}) as input (Figure 1 c). Under compositional training, we hide intermediate states from the inputs and for 1 ≤ t ≤ T 1\leq t\leq T train to predict s t s_{t} given ( s 0 , a 0 , a 1 , … , a t − 1 ) (s_{0},a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{t-1}) as input, forcing the model to compose actions internally with T T controlling the composition length. At T = 1 T=1 , next-state and compositional training coincide. 2.4 Measuring inference complexity of a transition with proof depth Certain held-out transitions are intuitively harder to infer than others. In the commutative world of Figure 4 , both held-out transitions are semantically entailed, but only one can be immediately derived from observed transitions; the other requires first inferring an intermediate transition. We quantify this dependency by proof depth, defined relative to a fixed set of inference rules based on the world’s algebraic constraints. Consider the rules of the commutative world depicted in Figure 4 b. Knowing transitions ( 1 , F , 0 ) , ( 0 , R , 2 ) (1,F,0),(0,R,2) , and ( 1 , R , 3 ) (1,R,3) derives ( 3 , F , 2 ) (3,F,2) since actions F F and R R commute, so the paths 1 → 𝐹 0 → 𝑅 2 1\xrightarrow{F}0\xrightarrow{R}2 and 1 → 𝑅 3 → 𝐹 2 1\xrightarrow{R}3\xrightarrow{F}2 must end at the same state. Constraint cascading then happens in rounds, each round using the derived transitions of previous rounds, then inference rules infer transitions (Figure 4 b). The minimal number of rounds to infer a transition is its proof depth. 3 Constraint propagation in controlled monoid worlds We construct monoid worlds with N = 1024 N=1024 states satisfying specified constraints and train models on 95 % 95\% of state-action transitions ( s , a , a ⁡ ( s ) ) (s,a,a(s)) such that the remaining 5 % 5\% of held-out transitions, which we evaluate model generalization on, are entailed by seen transitions and the world’s constraint. Unless stated otherwise, models have four layers of width 64 and train for 150 150 k steps at T = 2 T=2 with reported results averaged over five seeds. 3.1 Next-state training fails to propagate constraints Under a next-state objective, where intermediate states are shown, transformers on inverse worlds fail to generalize with accuracy at chance (Figure 1 d.1). Scaling model, world, and compute does not save next-state training, and models continue to fail at propagating inverse constraints (Appendix A ). Across attention, recurrent, and state-space architectures, next-state training T = 2 T=2 fails, indistinguishable from chance, at propagating inverse, commutative, composition, and periodicity constraints in their associated worlds (Figure 2 ). Only in the trivial copy world where actions are identical ( A = B A=B ) does next-state training generalize. We find a systematic “copy” failure mode of general constraint propagation by next-state trained models, where models behave as if every world were the copy world. Averaged across architectures and worlds, 64 % 64\% of incorrectly inferred unseen transitions are explained by copy propagation, assuming the unseen ( s , A , A ⁡ ( s ) ) (s,A,A(s)) transition matches seen ( s , B , B ⁡ ( s ) ) (s,B,B(s)) , although seen transitions contradict the A = B A=B constraint at almost every state (Appendix B ). These results suggest the next-state objective poorly propagates constraints from data. 3.2 Compositional training improves constraint propagation Figure 2: Across monoid worlds and architectures, compositional training generalizes better than next-state training with equal optimizer steps. Compositional objective propagates inverse, commutative, and composition constraints with average accuracy of 96 % 96\% , and copy at 100 % 100\% . Next-state training only succeeds on copy and fails on other tested families. Neither propagates periodicity. Points averaged over 5 seeds and bars show standard deviations. Under a compositional objective, where intermediate states are hidden, transformers successfully propagate inverse constraints, generalizing unseen transitions with ≥ 93 % \geq 93\% accuracy (Figure 1 d.1). We find a sharp jump in generalization of 98 % 98\% when varying the composition length from T = 1 T=1 , a reduction to next-state training, to T = 2 T=2 , when training first includes two-action compositions. Across architectures, compositional training at T = 2 T=2 enables models to propagate inverse, commutativity, and composition constraints with an average accuracy of 96 % 96\% and copy at 100 % 100\% (Figure 2 ). Extending composition length to T = 4 T=4 yields nearly identical generalization results of 96 % 96\% averaged over the same worlds (Appendix D ). Periodicity constraints, however, are not propagated by next-state or compositional training at T = 2 ​ or ​ 4 T=2\text{ or }4 . Across periodicity worlds A k = 1 A^{k}=1 for k = 3 , 4 , 5 k=3,4,5 , compositionally trained transformers at 1 ≤ T ≤ 8 1\leq T\leq 8 all fail to generalize, suggesting that the failure is not due to training paths too short to contain the constraint. Compositionally trained models also have reduced “copy” failure modes, hallucinating a copy constraint for 36 % 36\% of failures (Appendix B ). Compositional training fits observed transitions an order of magnitude earlier than it recovers held-out ones. On the inverse world, transformers learn 100 % 100\% of seen transitions at 1.2 1.2 k steps but achieve 50 % 50\% generalization at 16 16 k, approximately 13 13 times as many training steps, evidence of a grokking-like delay ( Power et al., 2022 ) . We explore learning and propagating constraints towards geometric generalization in world models trained on visual environments and relational generalization in LLMs trained on knowledge-based tasks. We identify domain-relevant constraints, which often hold only approximately, and build entailed hold-outs which test whether models propagate the constraints. 4.1 Geometric constraints in visual world models An agent moves (L)eft/(R)ight/(F)orward/(B)ackward through an AI2-THOR virtual environment, generating a dataset of observation-action paths of length T = 2 T=2 (Figure 3 a.1) ( Kolve et al., 2022 ) . Euclidean geometry imposes constraints on motion requiring that the final destination be independent of the order of translations: stepping forward and then right or right and then forward takes you to the same endpoint. Actions are also invertible since you can undo a previous action by stepping in the opposite direction. In environments with object collisions, these constraints do not hold for all states. We can compute these approximate constraints by identifying paths which start from the same initial observation and recording whether certain action sequences converge to the same endpoint observation. If two action sequences frequently ( ≥ 50 % \geq 50\% ) map between the same initial and terminal observations, we declare them an approximate constraint. We find the Euclidean constraints: inverse L ​ R = 1 LR=1 and commutativity F ​ R = R ​ F FR=RF , which hold roughly 80 % 80\% of the time. We hold out transitions ( obs , action , next obs ) (\text{obs},\text{action},\text{next obs}) that test propagation of inverse and commutative constraints. These hold-outs are taken at states away from object collisions where constraints are valid. Transformer world models are trained to predict the next observation given previous observations and actions. Accuracy is measured by choosing the observation in the dataset with the highest predicted likelihood. Since visual similarity may enable held-out recovery without learning geometric constraints, we compare to a baseline of shifting observation pixels. Under next-observation training, where intermediate observations are shown, world models poorly generalize inverse and commutative constraints, with an accuracy of only 50 % 50\% and 51 % 51\% , respectively, compared to the pixel-shift baseline of 41 % 41\% and 44 % 44\% (Figure 3 a.2, 3 a.3). Trained compositionally, hiding intermediate observations, world models achieve 83 % 83\% accuracy on inverse and 93 % 93\% on commutative constraints, averaging a + 38 % +38\% improvement over next-observation trained models. To examine recovery without visual shortcuts, we train transformers to predict the next state directly, instead of its observation. Generalization for next-state trained models on inverse and commutative constraints collapses to random guessing, while compositionally trained models achieve 94 % 94\% and 98 % 98\% , respectively (Figure 3 a.3). These results suggest next-observation/state training poorly propagates inverse and commutative constraints in visual domains while compositional training successfully propagates geometric constraints even without visual cues. 4.2 Relational constraints in large language models We examine when LLMs, trained on facts, propagate relational constraints without premises supplied in context. We study inverse constraints between successor and predecessor, the converse relation between parent and child, and the composition of parent and grandparent. Unlike inverse relations, converse relations branch, and the child of a parent may be a sibling, not necessarily a strict identity. For each constraint, we extract a Wikidata knowledge graph of 512 512 renamed individuals and associated relations (Figure 3 b.1). We hold out transitions ( person A , relation , person B ) (\text{person A},\text{relation},\text{person B}) jointly entailed by training transitions and constraint. For example, the observed relationship ( Dana , parent , Ines ) (\text{Dana},\text{parent},\text{Ines}) entails the held-out relationship ( Ines , child , Dana ) (\text{Ines},\text{child},\text{Dana}) under the converse constraint. We finetune pretrained base LLMs (270M to 4B parameters) with next-token prediction on natural-language sentences generated from (T=2) training paths. We compare two phrasings the same underlying path. Next-state phrasing allows models to condition on intermediate entities, e.g., “Dana’s parent is Ines, whose parent is Vera”, while compositional phrasing omits intermediate entities, “Dana’s parent’s parent is Vera” (Figure 3 b.2). Across attention, recurrent, and state-space architectures, compositionally trained models propagate non-trivial constraints to recover unseen data while next-state trained models do not. Compositional training also shows superior propagation in vision and language domains. Both objectives use identical path data, the only difference is that compositional training hides intermediate states. Global understanding therefore depends on how training requires local observations to be combined. Providing intermediate states encourages models to solve the task locally, while compositional training encourages integration across actions. Training objective, perhaps more than architecture or task domain, determines whether a model propagates certain constraints. Across monoid worlds, constraints that are (not) propagated are consistently (not) propagated across the disparate architectures tested. Similarly, constraints propagated compositionally in monoid worlds are also propagated by compositional approaches in visual and language domains. This pattern suggests that controlled monoid worlds capture general learning biases that extend to richer tasks and may provide simplified environments for understanding and designing better-propagating algorithms. Even when models propagate constraints, propagation is shallow, with generalization decreasing sharply with proof depth. Higher proof depth transitions are also recovered later and more slowly. Together with training dynamics, this suggests an internal process resembling a slow, inaccurate constraint cascade. Increasing composition length improves generalization to deeper consequences, suggesting that propagation reach depends on the organization of local information it learns from. Propagating constraint consequences deeply is essential for consistent information integration. 7 Related work LLMs often learn facts without propagating their consequences. The reversal curse shows that training on one direction of a relation can fail to recover its reverse ( Berglund et al., 2024 ) . Similar failures exist in implicit reasoning, where models poorly compose relations ( Balesni et al., 2025 ) . Changes to training can address individual failures such as reversal ( Ma et al., 2026 ) and composition ( Feng et al., 2025 ) have been proposed, but remain specialized. We frame these failures and improvements in the context of learning and propagating constraints. Across controlled monoid worlds, visual environments, and knowledge-based language tasks, we study how objective determines which constraints models propagate. We further measure how far consequences are propagated using proof depth and explore associated training dynamics. Accurate local predictions do not imply coherent global understanding ( Vafa et al., 2024 ) . Previous work improves consistency through reverse-prediction training ( Kwon et al., 2026 ) or architectural modifications that recover group structures in synthetic environments ( Keurti et al., 2023 ) . Our constraint propagation framework extends beyond group structure to include semantic constraints such as the converse relation between parent and child. Training without intermediate states has improved generalization in knowledge-graph embedding models ( Guu et al., 2015 ) and discouraged local prediction shortcuts in planning ( Bachmann and Nagarajan, 2024 ) . We study how training objective affects constraint propagation across architectures, visual environments, and language tasks. Compositional training improves propagation for many geometric and semantic constraints but fails on others. Even when immediate consequences are recovered, generalization decreases sharply with proof depth. Composition length increases propagation reach to higher proof depths, suggesting that how much local information models combine during training shapes how far they propagate what they learn. 8 Conclusion We frame global understanding as learning constraints from local observations and propagating their consequences deeply. Our monoid worlds provide controlled environments where generalization is entailed by observed data and unobserved global constraints. Across architectures, next-state training fails to propagate non-trivial constraints, while compositional training substantially improves propagation. We apply our constraint framing to visual and language tasks and find corresponding improvements under compositional-style objectives as well as regularities in which constraints propagate and under what conditions across domains. Deep propagation remains limited, though longer composition lengths help. These results suggest that global understanding requires training methods that encourage models to integrate local observations and deeply propagate their consequences.
